title: Simulating Natural Selection
beats: Earlier blobs had assigned birth/death chances; real selection comes from traits meeting an environment, so build one
Plane, daily food, blobs from home edge; zero food dies, one survives, two survives and replicates
Run with no mutations first: population grows then levels off near carrying capacity (~95)
Turn on a single trait, speed, with a stated cost (double speed, double energy); asks for predictions listing several outcomes
Run: higher speed wins; initial value was slower than optimal; first example of selection
Populations evolve, individuals do not (Pokemon aside)
Better competitors but smaller total population; selection is not for the good of the species
Add size (energy cube law, eat 20% smaller) and sense; costs justified, cost formula tied to kinetic energy
All three traits mutate; each creature is a dot in a 3D trait space
Speed changed even though its rule did not; sense, expected to be selected strongly, stays spread out
Selection does what it does regardless of what anyone thinks is best
Cut food to 10: population collapses even though food could feed 5-10
Rewind and drop one food every two days so the population can adapt
Big size drops, sense and speed gain value; expected efficiency to win, was wrong
Environment decides which creatures exist; evolution is not a march toward advanced creatures
Quick recap and preview of counterintuitive traits

metrics.misconception: yes: individuals evolve; selection acts for the good of the species; evolution marches toward advanced creatures
metrics.brute_force: no: but runs the no-mutation world first (1:05) as a baseline
metrics.examples: 4 runs: baseline, speed only, three traits, low food (failed then ramped); trait count grows 0 to 1 to 3
metrics.ending: Environment matters lesson, recap, teaser for counterintuitive traits

new_moves.name: presenter-surprised-on-camera
new_moves.what: Narrator states a prior expectation, then reports the sim contradicted it, three times

new_moves.name: ramp-the-change
new_moves.what: When an abrupt change kills the system, redo it gradually so the lesson is not an artifact
new_moves.evidence: 7:44 to 8:00 food reduced one piece every two days

new_moves.name: cost-with-every-benefit
new_moves.what: Each trait is introduced with a benefit and an energy cost together so no trait is obviously best

new_moves.name: anti-teleology-aside
new_moves.what: Stops mid-sim to rule out a likely misreading (individuals evolve, good of species)

theory: The video teaches by letting the world surprise both presenter and viewer, then drawing the lesson from the surprise rather than from a rule. Each trait ships with a benefit and a cost so no outcome is predictable, which makes the predict prompts genuine and the sim the argument.
velocity: Scene builder: every adjustable parameter gets a benefit and cost label so the learner cannot guess the winner
Orchestrator: run baseline with no variation before any variable is turned on
Voice: state an expectation aloud before each run, and say plainly when the run contradicts it
Learner model: ask for open-ended predictions (several listed outcomes) and track which the learner leans toward
Scene builder: when a change collapses the sim, offer a gradual ramp rather than ending the demo
quote: It doesn't care what I or anyone else thinks is best.
